claims.text: A combined standardized experimental and first-principles-calibrated molecular-dynamics approach can accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties in high-entropy alloys.
The combined approach can determine these thermodynamic properties efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family.
NiFeCoCr alloys and derivatives containing Pd additions constitute a high-entropy-alloy family.
The target NiFeCoCr-based alloys and their Pd-containing derivatives are single-phase and chemically disordered in the as-cast or homogenized state.
Pd can be used as an FCC-metal additive to tune the parent NiFeCoCr alloy.
Controlled DSC measurements can capture melting temperature and fusion enthalpy in the proposed high-entropy alloys.
High-pressure densitometry can accurately capture the volume change at melting in the proposed alloys.
Using inert atmospheres and controlled heating and cooling rates minimizes kinetic effects in the thermodynamic measurements.
Local atomic configurations and coordination-environment distributions govern configurational and vibrational entropy contributions at melting.
High-entropy alloys possess distributed energy landscapes that must be represented when interpreting their melting behavior.
Correlating microscopic disorder with measured macroscopic transitions through calibrated simulations reduces systematic errors relative to standalone experiments or simulations.
The integrated approach will reduce relative prediction errors to approximately 5–10% or less.
Standalone DSC or simulation methods typically have relative errors of 10–20% for the target properties.
Standalone methods often cannot separate configurational contributions from intrinsic phase-transformation energetics.
The approach is robust for chemically homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys over a wide composition range.
Phase segregation, decomposition, and kinetic delays can limit the applicability of the approach by obscuring equilibrium thermodynamic signals.
The approach is to be rejected if errors exceed 10% for more than 70% of tested alloys or if simulations systematically fail to reproduce experimental trends.
